sections.title: Definition and how lung fibrosis develops

blocks.text: **Interstitial lung disease (ILD)**, also called **diffuse parenchymal lung disease (DPLD)**, is an umbrella label for a mixed group of disorders that injure the lung **interstitium and/or alveolar spaces**. They are lumped together because they look alike clinically, physiologically and radiologically: varying amounts of **inflammation and fibrosis**, exertional breathlessness with or without cough, and a restrictive lung defect.

Despite the name, the process is not confined to the interstitium: alveoli, small airways and vessels can all be involved. As fibrosis advances, compliant lung is replaced by **stiff scar tissue**, the architecture is distorted and **gas exchange fails**. How reversible this is depends entirely on the specific diagnosis.

blocks.title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF): the definition to learn
items: A **progressive, fibrosing interstitial pneumonia** of **unknown cause**
Occurs in **adults** (rare before 50)
Linked to a **usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP)** pattern on **histology or HRCT**
It is a diagnosis of exclusion: **occupational, drug and connective tissue causes must be ruled out first**

blocks.text: **Pathogenesis of IPF:** the alveolar epithelium is injured again and again. The repair response becomes **unregulated**, so fibroblasts multiply and lay down excess extracellular matrix, with **surprisingly little inflammation**. The lung loses elasticity and its gas-exchange surface, ending in progressive respiratory failure. This explains why anti-inflammatory drugs fail in IPF and antifibrotics are used instead.

ILD is a **pattern, not a final diagnosis**. Infection (e.g. _Pneumocystis_, viral, TB), malignancy (lymphangitic carcinomatosis), pulmonary oedema and aspiration can all produce diffuse shadowing and must be excluded before labelling a patient with ILD.

sections.title: Etiology: known causes and IPF risk factors

blocks.title: Known causes of ILD
rows: Most often **bleomycin, methotrexate, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin**; also busulfan, mitomycin C, cyclophosphamide, gold, flecainide, sulfasalazine
Always take a full drug history; some reactions are dose-related (bleomycin, amiodarone)
Changes often limited to the irradiated field
Rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis, SLE, polymyositis/dermatomyositis, Sjögren syndrome
Lung disease can appear **before** the joint or skin disease
Mouldy hay (farmer’s lung), bird proteins (bird fancier’s lung), malt, mushroom compost
IPF and the other idiopathic interstitial pneumonias; sarcoidosis
Diagnosed only after the above are excluded

blocks.title: IPF: proposed triggers and risk factors
items: **Cigarette smoking**: strong association
Older age and **male sex** (about 2:1)
Suggested triggers: viruses (e.g. EBV), metal or wood dust, some drugs (antidepressants), **chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux**
Familial cases are rare, but genes controlling the fibrotic response probably matter

blocks.text: **Rheumatoid arthritis:** lung involvement causes roughly **10–20% of RA deaths**. Most appears within 5 years of the arthritis, but in 10–20% the lung disease comes first. **Pulmonary fibrosis is the commonest lung manifestation**, and **NSIP** is probably the commonest pattern. Systemic sclerosis causes ILD in about half of patients.

**Radiation:** acute radiation pneumonitis typically appears **6–12 weeks** after treatment, with cough and breathlessness, and responds to glucocorticoids. Chronic fibrosis can follow months later; once established it usually does **not** respond to steroids. Concurrent cytotoxic drugs worsen radiation injury.

History checklist in any suspected ILD: **drugs and radiotherapy**, **all past jobs** (asbestos, silica, coal, beryllium), **birds and mouldy material**, **CTD symptoms** (rash, arthritis, Raynaud’s, sicca, myalgia) and **smoking**, since some ILDs occur only in smokers.

Pocket Medicine says SLE and RA cause pleural disease more often than ILD. Davidson’s, the primary authority here, states that **pulmonary fibrosis is the commonest lung manifestation of RA**. Use Davidson’s answer in the exam.

Davidson’s classifies DPLD into **four groups**: (1) **known cause**, such as drugs or connective tissue disease; (2) **idiopathic interstitial pneumonias (IIPs)**, of which **IPF** is the most important and commonest; (3) **granulomatous DPLD**, mainly **sarcoidosis**; (4) **other rare forms**, e.g. lymphangioleiomyomatosis and histiocytosis X. IIPs account for roughly 40% of DPLD.

blocks.note: Look at: the DPLD classification tree, with the IIP branch split into IPF and the six other IIPs.

blocks.title: Idiopathic interstitial pneumonias compared
rows: UIP (patchy fibrosis, fibroblastic foci, subpleural honeycombing)
Older men, smokers; basal subpleural honeycombing
Antifibrotics, not steroids; median survival about 3 years
Younger, often women; linked to CTD, drugs, chronic HP, HIV; more ground glass, little honeycombing
Steroids ± azathioprine or cyclophosphamide; 5-year mortality usually <15%
Organising pneumonia: buds of immature collagen (**Masson bodies**)
Pneumonia-like illness, systemic upset, very high ESR, **no clubbing**; patchy, migratory peripheral consolidation
Excellent, rapid steroid response; relapses common
Viral-type prodrome, then respiratory failure over days to weeks
Pulsed IV methylprednisolone then oral steroids; poor prognosis
Pigmented macrophages filling the alveolar spaces
Smokers aged 40–60, men > women; clubbing in about 50%; widespread ground glass
Current or ex-smokers; centrilobular nodules, upper-lobe predominant
Middle-aged women; CTD or HIV; ground glass with perivascular cysts

blocks.text: **IPF and UIP are not synonyms.** UIP is the histological pattern of IPF, but the same pattern occurs in **asbestosis, chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, connective tissue disease and drug reactions**. A UIP biopsy therefore does not prove IPF until those causes are excluded.

blocks.title: Other important ILDs
items: **Sarcoidosis**: multisystem disorder of unknown cause with **non-caseating granulomas**; the lungs are involved in over 90%. CXR stages: I hilar nodes only, II nodes + parenchymal disease, III parenchymal only, IV fibrosis

**Hypersensitivity pneumonitis** (extrinsic allergic alveolitis): an immune reaction (type III with cell-mediated components) of small airways and alveoli to an inhaled antigen. Examples are farmer’s lung (thermophilic actinomycetes in mouldy hay) and bird fancier’s lung. Smokers have a lower risk. BAL shows lymphocytosis; treat by removing the antigen ± steroids
**Asbestosis**: **lower-lobe** fibrosis appearing **>15–20 years** after exposure; **pleural plaques** are the clue; raised risk of lung cancer (synergy with smoking) and mesothelioma
**Silicosis**: **upper-lobe** nodular fibrosis, **eggshell calcification** of hilar nodes, raised **TB** risk
**Chronic berylliosis**: mimics sarcoidosis (granulomas, skin lesions, hypercalcaemia); beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test

blocks.text: Smoking-related IIPs are **DIP and RB-ILD**: both show pigmented (smoker’s) macrophages, both mainly affect men, and the key treatment for both is **stopping smoking**.
In hypersensitivity pneumonitis, serum **precipitating antibodies show exposure, not disease**. Many exposed people without symptoms are positive.

blocks.note: Look at: UIP. Subpleural scarring down the posterior lower lobe (honeycomb lung) and histology of dense fibrosis with honeycomb cysts.
Look at: non-caseating granulomas of pulmonary sarcoidosis.

blocks.title: Symptoms common to DPLD
items: **Breathlessness**: insidious, then relentlessly progressive, first on exertion and later at rest (acute in a few types)
**Cough**: usually **dry**, persistent and distressing
Fatigue; constitutional symptoms are unusual in IPF

blocks.title: Signs
items: **Fine, late-inspiratory, bilateral basal crackles** that sound like Velcro being pulled apart
**Finger clubbing**: common in IPF and asbestosis, often a late sign
Advanced disease: **central cyanosis**, **pulmonary hypertension** and **right heart failure** (loud P2, peripheral oedema)

blocks.title: Typical IPF patient
rows: Men about twice as often as women
Gradual onset over months (more than 3 months in most)
Present in a large minority to most patients (figures vary between books from 25–50% to about two-thirds)
Steady decline, punctuated by acute exacerbations

blocks.title: Clues that point away from IPF
items: **Acute onset** (days to weeks): think infection, heart failure, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, eosinophilic pneumonia, AIP, COP or a drug reaction
**Extrapulmonary features**: rash, arthritis, myalgia, sicca symptoms, alopecia or Raynaud’s suggest a connective tissue disease

blocks.text: **Course and complications of IPF:** decline is usually steady, but **acute exacerbations** cause sudden worsening breathlessness and gas exchange with **new ground glass or consolidation on HRCT**, and they raise mortality. Stepwise falls also follow **pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism or infection**. Late disease brings pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale and respiratory failure. Davidson’s quotes a **median survival of about 3 years**, with very wide variation between patients.

blocks.title: Markers of a worse prognosis in IPF
items: Markedly **reduced gas transfer** and/or **desaturation on exercise**
An early **fall in FVC or TLCO** after diagnosis
Many **fibroblastic foci** on biopsy

blocks.text: Bibasal crackles in an older breathless patient are often put down to **heart failure or recurrent chest infection**, which delays the diagnosis of IPF. Clubbing and a dry cough with "Velcro" crackles should prompt HRCT.

The books disagree. Survival: Davidson’s median about 3 years, Kumar 2–5 years, KC Essentials about 5 years, Step-Up a mean of 3–7 years. Cough: Davidson’s says non-productive, Kumar allows sputum. For exams, quote Davidson’s: **dry cough, median survival about 3 years**.

blocks.note: Look at: finger clubbing (enlarged, bulbous fingertip), a common and often late sign of fibrotic ILD, especially IPF.

blocks.title: Pulmonary function in ILD (restrictive pattern)
rows: Airways are not obstructed; fibrosis may even pull them open
Hypoxaemia with low or normal PaCO2
Gas-exchange failure drives hyperventilation, so CO2 is not retained in the typical picture

blocks.text: Normal spirometry does **not** exclude ILD. It can be normal early, and **coexisting emphysema** can keep lung volumes near normal, so the low gas transfer may be the only clue. A mixed restrictive and obstructive pattern suggests sarcoidosis.

blocks.title: Imaging
items: **CXR**: small-volume lungs with bilateral **lower-zone, subpleural reticular** shadowing; may be **normal** in early disease

**HRCT** is the investigation of choice. Confident IPF features are **basal** predominance, **subpleural reticulation**, **traction bronchiectasis** and **honeycombing** (clustered thick-walled cysts)
When those UIP features are present, HRCT has a **high positive predictive value for IPF**, so **biopsy is seldom needed**
**Pleural plaques** point to asbestosis; HRCT can also suggest HP or sarcoidosis

blocks.title: HRCT distribution as a diagnostic clue
rows: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis, silicosis, coal, sarcoidosis, smoking-related ILD, Langerhans cell histiocytosis

blocks.title: Blood tests
items: **FBC**: lymphopenia (sarcoid), eosinophilia (eosinophilic or drug lung disease), neutrophilia (hypersensitivity pneumonitis)
**Calcium and ACE**: raised in sarcoid (ACE is non-specific); **LDH** may rise in active alveolitis; ESR/CRP raised non-specifically
**Autoimmune screen**: ANA, RF, anti-CCP, plus targeted tests (e.g. Scl-70, SSA/SSB, ANCA, CK and myositis antibodies)
No blood test is specific for IPF. A **weakly positive ANA or anti-CCP is common**, and serology may be repeated because lung disease can precede CTD

blocks.title: Bronchoscopy and biopsy
items: **BAL** mainly to exclude **infection or malignancy**. Lymphocytosis suggests **HP**, neutrophils >3% are usual in **IPF**, and a **raised CD4:CD8 ratio** suggests **sarcoidosis**
**Transbronchial biopsy** samples are too small to diagnose IPF but are useful for sarcoid, infection and malignancy
**Surgical lung biopsy (usually VATS)** is the most reliable way to obtain histology. Reserve it for **atypical or uncertain** cases

blocks.alt: Algorithm: clinical assessment, CXR, PFTs and bloods lead to HRCT. A typical UIP pattern gives a diagnosis of IPF; a pattern of another DPLD is confirmed and treated; atypical findings go to BAL or transbronchial/surgical biopsy.

blocks.text: Ground glass is an **early or inflammatory** change. When it **dominates** the HRCT, think of **NSIP, HP, DIP or AIP** rather than IPF, whose hallmark is reticulation with honeycombing.

blocks.note: Look at: the ILD investigation algorithm, where HRCT is the branch point after clinical assessment, CXR, PFTs and bloods.
Look at: HRCT of IPF with bilateral, basal, peripheral reticular opacities and honeycombing.
Look at: subpleural reticulation and honeycombing at both lung bases in IPF.

blocks.title: Antifibrotic drugs
rows: **Photosensitive rash** (avoid sun, high-factor sunscreen), GI upset

blocks.title: Rules for antifibrotic therapy (Davidson’s)
items: Offer when **vital capacity is 50–80% predicted**
They **slow the decline in lung function (FVC)** but **do not improve cough or breathlessness**
**Stop** if lung function falls by **more than 10% during the first year** of treatment
Monitor with **serial lung function tests**

blocks.title: Supportive care
items: **Stop smoking** (also raises lung cancer risk)
**Influenza and pneumococcal** vaccination
**Pulmonary rehabilitation** and exercise, with ambulatory oxygen if needed
**Home oxygen** to palliate breathlessness in severe disease or when hypoxic at rest
**Anti-reflux treatment** for symptomatic GORD, which may ease the cough
Screen for pulmonary hypertension; **lung transplant assessment**; **advance care planning and palliative care**

blocks.text: **Acute exacerbation of IPF:** no treatment has proven benefit and care is largely **supportive**. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are often given, sometimes with high-dose glucocorticoids or other immunosuppression, but the evidence is weak.

Classic trap: **corticosteroids and immunosuppression are not used in confirmed IPF**. They were used in the past, gave little or no benefit and caused significant harm. Antifibrotics are the disease-modifying option.

Contrast with other ILDs that **do** respond to steroids: **COP** (excellent), **cellular NSIP**, **AIP** (pulsed IV methylprednisolone), **acute radiation pneumonitis** and drug-induced pneumonitis after the drug is stopped. DIP and RB-ILD need **smoking cessation** above all.
Nintedanib is a **small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor**, not a monoclonal antibody, despite what one revision source says.

cards.back: A progressive fibrosing interstitial pneumonia of unknown cause in adults, with a **UIP pattern** on histology or HRCT, after occupational, drug and CTD causes are excluded.

cards.front: Core mechanism of fibrosis in IPF?
cards.back: Repeated alveolar epithelial injury, then **unregulated repair**: fibroblast proliferation and matrix deposition with **little inflammation**.

cards.front: The four drugs that most often cause pulmonary fibrosis (Davidson’s)?
Commonest lung manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis, and its usual pattern?
When does acute radiation pneumonitis typically appear?
cards.back: **6–12 weeks** after radiotherapy; it responds to glucocorticoids, unlike established post-radiation fibrosis.

cards.front: Histological hallmark and steroid response of cryptogenic organising pneumonia?
cards.back: **Masson bodies** (buds of immature collagen in alveoli and ducts); the steroid response is classically **excellent**, but relapses are common.

cards.front: Besides IPF, where else is a UIP pattern found?
cards.back: **Asbestosis, chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, connective tissue disease, drug reactions**.

cards.front: Which two IIPs are smoking-related, and what is their key treatment?
Widely quoted median survival of IPF (Davidson’s)?
cards.back: About **3 years**, with very variable progression.
**Restrictive**: FEV1 and FVC both low, **FEV1/FVC normal or raised**, low lung volumes and **low TLCO** (often the earliest change).

cards.front: Four HRCT features for a confident diagnosis of IPF?
Davidson’s criteria to start and stop antifibrotics in IPF?
cards.back: Start if **VC 50–80% predicted**; stop if lung function falls **>10% in the first year**.

questions.stem: A respiratory registrar is explaining to a student why a 70-year-old man with progressive breathlessness has been labelled as having idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis rather than "pulmonary fibrosis, cause to be found".
questions.leadIn: Which feature is part of the definition of IPF?
options: A usual interstitial pneumonia pattern on HRCT or histology
A documented history of asbestos exposure
Onset of symptoms before the age of 40
questions.explanation: IPF is a progressive fibrosing interstitial pneumonia of unknown cause in adults, linked to a **UIP pattern** on histology or HRCT. Known causes (occupational, drug, CTD) must be excluded first.
whyNot: Granulomas suggest sarcoidosis or HP, not IPF.
A known exposure such as asbestos makes the fibrosis secondary (asbestosis), so it is not idiopathic.
Strongly positive CTD serology points to CTD-associated ILD; only weak positives are common in IPF.
IPF is uncommon before 50; young onset argues against it.

questions.stem: A student asks why prednisolone, which helps many inflammatory lung conditions, is ineffective in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
questions.leadIn: Which mechanism best explains the fibrosis in IPF?
options: Unregulated repair of repeatedly injured alveolar epithelium with little inflammation
Immune-complex deposition triggered by an inhaled organic antigen
Formation of non-caseating granulomas around a persistent antigen
Eosinophilic infiltration of the alveoli in response to a drug
Antibodies directed against the alveolar basement membrane
questions.explanation: In IPF the epithelium is injured repeatedly and the wound-healing response runs out of control: fibroblasts proliferate and lay down matrix with **little inflammation**. This is why anti-inflammatory therapy fails and antifibrotics are used.
whyNot: This describes hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
This describes sarcoidosis.
This describes drug-induced pulmonary eosinophilia.
This describes Goodpasture disease.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has had 9 months of increasing exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. His medicines are amiodarone (for 3 years), bisoprolol, apixaban, digoxin and atorvastatin. He has fine bibasal crackles, and HRCT shows bilateral reticulation.
questions.leadIn: Which of his medicines is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: **Amiodarone** is one of the four drugs that most often cause pulmonary fibrosis (with bleomycin, methotrexate and nitrofurantoin). Management is to stop the drug; steroids are often given.
whyNot: Beta-blockers cause bronchospasm (asthma), not interstitial fibrosis.
An anticoagulant; its main risk is bleeding, not ILD.
Not among the drugs listed as causing pulmonary fibrosis or alveolitis.
Not among the drugs listed as causing pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis for 4 years develops progressive breathlessness. HRCT shows bilateral lower-zone interstitial changes.
questions.leadIn: Which interstitial pattern is most likely?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary fibrosis is the commonest lung manifestation of RA. All ILD patterns occur, but **NSIP is probably the most common**.
whyNot: UIP does occur in RA, but NSIP is the more common pattern.
DIP is a smoking-related IIP.
LIP is linked to CTD and HIV, but NSIP is the commonest ILD pattern in RA.
AIP is an acute illness with diffuse alveolar damage, not a gradual RA-associated fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has had fever, malaise, cough and breathlessness for 4 weeks despite two courses of antibiotics. ESR is 105 mm/h. There is no clubbing. Serial CT scans show patchy peripheral consolidation that changes position between scans. A lung biopsy shows buds of immature collagen plugging the alveolar ducts.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pneumonia-like illness unresponsive to antibiotics, a very high ESR, no clubbing, **migratory peripheral consolidation** and **Masson bodies** on biopsy are classic for **COP**. It responds rapidly to steroids, though relapse is common.
whyNot: IPF is insidious, often with clubbing, and shows basal reticulation and honeycombing rather than migratory consolidation.
AIP causes respiratory failure over days to weeks, with diffuse alveolar damage on biopsy.
DIP affects smokers, and its biopsy shows pigmented macrophages filling the alveoli.
LIP has a slow onset over years, with ground glass and perivascular cysts.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old male smoker (30 per day) has had slowly increasing breathlessness for several months. He has finger clubbing. HRCT shows widespread ground-glass opacification without centrilobular nodules. Lung biopsy shows the alveolar spaces packed with pigmented macrophages.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A middle-aged male smoker with clubbing (about 50% in DIP), widespread ground glass and **pigmented macrophages filling the alveoli** fits **DIP**. Stopping smoking is the key treatment and the outlook is generally good.
whyNot: In RB-ILD the macrophages are mainly in the respiratory bronchioles, and HRCT shows centrilobular nodules.
IPF shows a UIP pattern with fibrosis and honeycombing, not alveoli filled with macrophages.
COP shows Masson bodies and migratory consolidation.
Sarcoidosis shows non-caseating granulomas.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old retired accountant has 18 months of progressive exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. He has finger clubbing.
questions.leadIn: Which chest finding on auscultation is most expected?
options: Fine late-inspiratory crackles at both bases
Coarse early-inspiratory crackles that clear on coughing
Bronchial breathing over the right upper zone
A pleural friction rub at the left base
questions.explanation: IPF classically gives **fine, late-inspiratory, bibasal "Velcro" crackles**, often with clubbing.
whyNot: Coarse crackles that change with coughing suggest secretions (e.g. bronchiectasis), not fibrosis.
Wheeze indicates airflow obstruction (asthma or COPD), not fibrosis.
Bronchial breathing indicates consolidation.
A rub indicates pleural inflammation.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman has just been diagnosed with IPF. She asks what might suggest that her disease will progress quickly.
questions.leadIn: Which finding predicts a poorer prognosis?
options: Markedly reduced gas transfer with desaturation on exercise
questions.explanation: Significantly **impaired gas transfer** and/or **exercise desaturation** herald a poorer prognosis, as do an early fall in FVC or TLCO and many fibroblastic foci on biopsy.
whyNot: Relatively preserved lung function suggests longer survival.
A weakly positive ANA is common in IPF and is not a marker of prognosis.
ACE is a non-specific marker of sarcoid activity.
Clubbing is not used as a prognostic marker.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with suspected fibrotic interstitial lung disease has full pulmonary function tests.
questions.leadIn: Which set of results is most consistent with ILD?
options: FEV1 reduced, FVC reduced, FEV1/FVC 0.86, TLCO reduced
FEV1 reduced, FVC normal, FEV1/FVC 0.55, TLCO reduced
FEV1 reduced, FVC reduced, FEV1/FVC 0.85, TLCO raised
FEV1 normal, FVC normal, FEV1/FVC 0.80, TLCO normal
FEV1 reduced, FVC normal, FEV1/FVC 0.60, TLCO normal
questions.explanation: ILD gives a **restrictive** defect: FEV1 and FVC both fall, so the **ratio is normal or raised**, and **gas transfer is reduced** because the alveolar–capillary membrane is thickened.
whyNot: A low ratio with low TLCO is obstruction with emphysema.
Gas transfer falls in ILD; a raised TLCO points away from fibrosis.
Normal results do not fit established fibrotic disease (though spirometry can be normal very early).
A low ratio with normal TLCO is obstruction, e.g. asthma.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man has 2 years of progressive breathlessness. HRCT is performed to identify the type of ILD.
questions.leadIn: Which HRCT appearance most strongly supports IPF?
options: Basal subpleural reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis
Upper-zone centrilobular nodules with air trapping
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with perilymphatic nodules
Patchy peripheral consolidation that migrates between scans
Widespread ground glass with sparing of the subpleural lung
questions.explanation: Confident IPF (UIP) features are **basal**, **subpleural reticulation**, **traction bronchiectasis** and **honeycombing**. When present, HRCT has a high positive predictive value and biopsy is seldom needed.
whyNot: Upper-zone nodules with air trapping suggest hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
Hilar nodes with perilymphatic nodules suggest sarcoidosis.
Migratory consolidation suggests COP.
Ground glass with subpleural sparing suggests NSIP.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with confirmed IPF and an FVC of 65% predicted starts an antifibrotic drug. He is advised to avoid direct sunlight and use a high-protection sunscreen.
questions.leadIn: Which drug has he most likely been started on?
questions.explanation: **Pirfenidone** causes **photosensitivity** (and GI upset), so sun protection is advised. Nintedanib commonly causes diarrhoea.
whyNot: Nintedanib is the other antifibrotic; its typical side effect is diarrhoea.
Steroids are not used in confirmed IPF.
Immunosuppression is generally avoided in IPF.
Methotrexate is not an IPF treatment and is itself a cause of pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman has IPF confirmed at a multidisciplinary meeting. Her vital capacity is 68% predicted. She asks what treatment can alter the course of the disease.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate disease-modifying option?
questions.explanation: With VC **50–80% predicted**, an antifibrotic (**nintedanib** or pirfenidone) is offered to slow the decline in lung function. Steroids and immunosuppressants are not used in confirmed IPF.
whyNot: Steroids are no longer recommended in confirmed IPF: little benefit, significant harm.
Immunosuppression is generally avoided in IPF.
Cyclophosphamide is used in some NSIP, not IPF.
Hydroxychloroquine has no role in IPF.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man who keeps racing pigeons has recurrent episodes of fever, dry cough and breathlessness starting a few hours after he cleans the loft. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows a marked lymphocytosis.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Symptoms a few hours after antigen exposure (bird proteins) with **BAL lymphocytosis** are typical of **hypersensitivity pneumonitis (bird fancier’s lung)**. Treatment is antigen avoidance ± steroids.
whyNot: IPF is steadily progressive and not linked to exposures.
Sarcoid is not exposure-linked; BAL shows a high CD4:CD8 ratio.
COP is a subacute pneumonia-like illness without exposure-linked attacks.
DIP affects heavy smokers and is not episodic.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman with Raynaud’s phenomenon and puffy fingers has 8 months of exertional breathlessness. HRCT shows symmetrical basal ground-glass opacification with fine reticulation and minimal honeycombing.
questions.leadIn: Which interstitial pattern is most likely?
questions.explanation: A younger woman with CTD features and **ground glass with little honeycombing** fits **NSIP**. Its prognosis is much better than IPF, and it responds to steroids ± immunosuppression.
whyNot: UIP is more typical of older men, with prominent honeycombing.
AIP is an acute illness over days to weeks.
RB-ILD occurs in smokers, with centrilobular nodules.
COP causes migratory consolidation with a pneumonia-like illness.

questions.stem: A previously well 50-year-old man has a flu-like illness, then rapidly worsening breathlessness over 10 days and needs high-flow oxygen. HRCT shows diffuse ground glass with consolidation and traction bronchiectasis. Cultures and echocardiography are unremarkable.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A viral prodrome followed by respiratory failure over **days to weeks**, with diffuse alveolar damage, is **AIP (Hamman–Rich syndrome)**. It is treated with pulsed IV methylprednisolone, and the prognosis is poor.
whyNot: IPF is insidious over months to years.
NSIP runs a subacute to chronic course.
DIP develops insidiously in smokers.
LIP develops slowly over years.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman has a dry cough and mild breathlessness. HRCT shows hilar lymphadenopathy and perilymphatic nodules. Blood tests are being reviewed.
questions.leadIn: Which combination of blood results would most support the likely diagnosis?
options: Strongly positive anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor
questions.explanation: In the DPLD blood screen, **lymphopenia** and **raised calcium** (± raised ACE) point to **sarcoidosis**, which fits the hilar nodes and perilymphatic nodules.
whyNot: Neutrophilia with precipitins suggests hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
Eosinophilia suggests pulmonary eosinophilia or a drug reaction.
Raised CK with myositis antibodies suggests myositis-associated ILD.
Strong RA serology suggests rheumatoid lung disease.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has progressive breathlessness. HRCT shows fibrosis with an atypical distribution that does not fit UIP or any other recognisable pattern. The team decides tissue is needed.
questions.leadIn: Which procedure is most likely to give a diagnostic sample?
questions.explanation: **Surgical lung biopsy, usually by VATS**, is the most reliable way to obtain enough tissue to classify fibrotic ILD. It is reserved for atypical or uncertain cases.
whyNot: Transbronchial samples are too small to diagnose UIP/IPF, though useful for sarcoid.
BAL gives cells, not architecture; it mainly excludes infection or malignancy.
Bronchial biopsy samples airway mucosa; only occasionally useful in sarcoid.
Sputum cytology has no role in classifying fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with IPF started pirfenidone a year ago, when his FVC was 72% predicted. At his 12-month review his FVC is 58% predicted, with no infection or other cause for the fall.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate action regarding pirfenidone?
questions.explanation: Davidson’s advises **stopping antifibrotic treatment** if lung function falls by **more than 10% over the first year**. That has happened here.
whyNot: Steroids are not used in IPF.
Dose escalation beyond the licensed dose is not a recognised strategy.
Immunosuppression is avoided in IPF.
Continuing is inappropriate once the stopping threshold is passed.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man has been treated with furosemide for "heart failure" for 18 months without improvement. His echocardiogram is normal. He has a dry cough, finger clubbing and fine late-inspiratory bibasal crackles.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bibasal crackles are often misread as heart failure or infection, delaying the diagnosis of IPF. A normal echo, clubbing, dry cough and "Velcro" crackles in an older man point to **IPF**.
whyNot: A normal echo and no diuretic response argue against heart failure.
Bronchiectasis gives copious purulent sputum and coarse crackles.
COPD causes airflow obstruction (low FEV1/FVC), and clubbing is not a feature of COPD.
Sarcoid usually affects younger adults, and auscultation is often surprisingly normal.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old former shipyard insulation worker has progressive breathlessness. HRCT shows lower-zone subpleural fibrosis and calcified pleural plaques. A biopsy taken elsewhere was reported as a "UIP pattern".
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: UIP is not specific for IPF; it also occurs in **asbestosis**. A long latency after occupational exposure, lower-zone fibrosis and **pleural plaques** make asbestosis the diagnosis. IPF requires known causes to be excluded.
whyNot: An exposure that explains the fibrosis rules out an "idiopathic" diagnosis, and plaques point to asbestos.
Silicosis is upper-lobe and nodular, with eggshell nodal calcification.
There is no organic antigen history, and HP tends to affect the upper zones.
Sarcoid shows granulomas, not UIP, and does not cause pleural plaques.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old ex-smoker has 14 months of progressive breathlessness and a dry cough. He takes no regular medicines and has no occupational dust exposure, birds or joint, skin or muscle symptoms. He has clubbing and fine bibasal crackles. PFTs: FVC 70% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.84, TLCO 48%. HRCT: basal-predominant subpleural reticulation, honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis. ANA is weakly positive at 1:80.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step in establishing the diagnosis?
options: Surgical lung biopsy before any diagnosis
Diagnose CTD-associated ILD and start prednisolone
questions.explanation:
**Step 1, is it ILD?** Progressive breathlessness, dry cough, clubbing and Velcro crackles, plus a restrictive defect (normal ratio, low TLCO). Yes.
**Step 2, any known cause?** No drugs, dusts, birds or CTD features. A weakly positive ANA is common in IPF and does not make it CTD-ILD.
**Step 3, what does HRCT show?** All four confident UIP features (basal, subpleural reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, honeycombing). These have a **high positive predictive value for IPF**, so **biopsy is seldom needed**.
**Conclusion:** diagnose IPF. With VC 50–80%, he is eligible for an antifibrotic.
whyNot: Surgical biopsy is reserved for atypical or uncertain cases; this HRCT is typical.
Transbronchial samples are too small to diagnose IPF.
A low-titre ANA with no clinical CTD features is common in IPF; steroids are not used.
BAL is mainly to exclude infection or malignancy and cannot confirm IPF.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man completed chemotherapy for a germ cell tumour 4 months ago. His regimen included bleomycin, cisplatin and etoposide, with ondansetron and dexamethasone for nausea. He now has progressive exertional breathlessness, a dry cough and fine basal crackles. PFTs show a restrictive pattern with reduced gas transfer.
questions.leadIn: Which drug is most likely responsible for his lung disease?
questions.explanation:
**Step 1, recognise the syndrome:** restrictive physiology, low gas transfer and crackles = ILD.
**Step 2, scan the drug list:** of his drugs, only **bleomycin** is among the four that most often cause pulmonary fibrosis (bleomycin, methotrexate, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin).
**Step 3, note the mechanism:** bleomycin lung toxicity is dose-related, so cumulative dose matters.
**Take-home:** in any new ILD, take a full drug history, including past chemotherapy and radiotherapy.
whyNot: Cisplatin is not among the cytotoxics listed as causing pulmonary fibrosis.
Etoposide is not a listed cause of drug-induced fibrosis.
An antiemetic with no recognised link to ILD.
A glucocorticoid; it would, if anything, suppress pneumonitis.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman with IPF (VC 66% predicted) has been on nintedanib for 6 months. Her lung function is stable, but her cough remains troublesome. She also has heartburn and acid regurgitation after meals.
questions.leadIn: Which additional measure is most likely to improve her cough?
questions.explanation:
**Step 1:** recall what antifibrotics do. They **slow FVC decline** but **do not improve cough or breathlessness**, so changing or adding an antifibrotic will not help the cough.
**Step 2:** look for a treatable contributor. She has symptomatic **GORD**, which is linked to IPF and may drive further epithelial injury. Treating reflux **may improve the cough**.
**Step 3:** avoid the trap. Steroids and immunosuppression are not used in IPF.
whyNot: Antifibrotics do not improve cough, and her lung function is stable.
Combining antifibrotics does not address cough.
Steroids are not recommended in confirmed IPF.
Immunosuppression is avoided in IPF.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the type of ILD they most likely have. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 51-year-old woman with long-standing HIV infection has had slowly worsening breathlessness and a dry cough over 3 years. HRCT shows ground-glass opacification with scattered thin-walled perivascular cysts.
items.explanation: **LIP**: a middle-aged woman with HIV (or CTD), insidious onset, ground glass and **perivascular cysts**. Treat with steroids, plus antiretrovirals in HIV.

items.stem: A 36-year-old non-smoking teacher has a dry cough. HRCT shows nodules along the bronchovascular bundles. Her serum calcium is raised and she is lymphopenic. BAL shows a lymphocytosis with a CD4:CD8 ratio of 7.
items.explanation: Two steps. The bloods (hypercalcaemia, lymphopenia) suggest sarcoid, and a **raised CD4:CD8 ratio** on BAL separates **sarcoidosis** from HP, which also gives a lymphocytosis.

items.stem: A 50-year-old dairy farmer gets fever, chills, cough and breathlessness about 6 hours after forking stored hay in winter. He is well in between. BAL shows a marked lymphocytosis.
items.explanation: Symptoms hours after exposure to mouldy hay (thermophilic actinomycetes) = **farmer’s lung**, a form of **hypersensitivity pneumonitis**.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man smokes 25 cigarettes a day and has a mild cough and breathlessness. HRCT shows upper-lobe centrilobular nodules, bronchial wall thickening and patchy ground glass. Bronchoscopic samples show pigmented macrophages in the respiratory bronchioles.
items.explanation: A current smoker with **centrilobular nodules** and pigmented macrophages in the **respiratory bronchioles** = **RB-ILD**. Treat by stopping smoking. (In DIP the macrophages fill the alveoli diffusely.)

questions.stem: A student is comparing physical signs across the diffuse parenchymal lung diseases.
questions.leadIn: In which condition is finger clubbing characteristically absent?
questions.explanation: Davidson’s notes that clubbing is **absent in COP**, which helps separate it from fibrotic ILDs. This fits COP’s subacute, pneumonia-like course.
whyNot: Clubbing is common in IPF.
Clubbing is also seen in asbestosis.
About 50% of patients with DIP are clubbed.
Clubbing may be present in chronic HP.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with advanced IPF is breathless at rest. Arterial blood gases are taken on room air.
questions.leadIn: Which pattern is most expected?
questions.explanation: As IPF advances, **hypoxaemia with hypocapnia** appears at rest. Breathlessness drives hyperventilation, so CO2 is low (or normal), not raised.
whyNot: Type 2 failure (raised CO2) is not the typical pattern of ILD.
Advanced IPF causes hypoxaemia; isolated hypercapnia suggests hypoventilation.
Gases are normal at rest only in early disease.
A high PaO2 on room air is not physiological here.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman develops a dry cough and breathlessness 8 weeks after completing radiotherapy to the chest. CT shows ground glass and consolidation sharply confined to the radiotherapy field.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Cough and breathlessness **6–12 weeks** after radiotherapy, with changes limited to the irradiated area = **acute radiation pneumonitis**. It may resolve spontaneously and responds to glucocorticoids.
whyNot: Chronic fibrosis appears months later and usually does not respond to steroids.
IPF is bilateral, basal and insidious, not confined to a radiation field.
Secondary organising pneumonia is possible, but the timing and geometric field make radiation pneumonitis likelier.
Lymphangitic spread is bilateral and does not follow a treatment field.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with known IPF has 6 days of rapidly worsening breathlessness. HRCT shows new bilateral ground glass on a background of honeycombing. Pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax and infection have been excluded.
questions.leadIn: Which statement about this complication is correct?
options: No treatment has proven benefit and care is largely supportive
High-dose steroids are proven effective in randomised trials
Most patients recover to their previous baseline
It occurs in NSIP but not in IPF
Survival is unaffected by the episode
questions.explanation: This is an **acute exacerbation of IPF**. No treatment is proven, so care is mainly supportive; antibiotics ± steroids are often given on little evidence. Mortality rises after exacerbations, and failure to regain baseline is common.
whyNot: There are no RCT data supporting high-dose steroids.
Failure to return to baseline after such episodes is common.
Acute exacerbations are a well-recognised feature of IPF.
Acute exacerbations are associated with increased mortality.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old former sandblaster has exertional breathlessness. CXR shows nodular fibrosis in both upper zones and eggshell calcification of the hilar lymph nodes.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **Silicosis**: upper-lobe nodular fibrosis with **eggshell calcification** of nodes, after sandblasting, mining or stone cutting. It raises the risk of **tuberculosis**.
whyNot: Asbestosis is lower-lobe, with pleural plaques.
Berylliosis mimics sarcoid (granulomas, hypercalcaemia) and follows beryllium exposure.
IPF is basal, with no causative exposure.
Sarcoid does not follow dust exposure, and eggshell calcification is the classic silica sign.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman has progressive breathlessness. She also has Raynaud’s phenomenon, thickened skin over the fingers and difficulty swallowing. HRCT shows basal interstitial changes.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely underlying cause of her lung disease?
questions.explanation: Raynaud’s, sclerodactyly and dysphagia indicate **systemic sclerosis**, which causes ILD in about half of patients. Look for extrapulmonary CTD clues in every ILD.
whyNot: RA would give a symmetrical inflammatory arthritis.
SLE more often causes pleurisy and effusions, and the skin features here fit scleroderma.
Sarcoid does not cause sclerodactyly or dysphagia.
IPF requires CTD to be excluded, and here it clearly is present.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman has a dry cough. HRCT shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and perilymphatic nodules. Bronchoalveolar lavage is performed.
questions.leadIn: Which BAL finding would most support the likely diagnosis?
options: Lymphocytosis with a raised CD4:CD8 ratio
Lymphocytosis with mast cells after bird exposure
Milky fluid rich in surfactant-like material
questions.explanation: Hilar nodes with perilymphatic nodules suggest **sarcoidosis**, where BAL typically shows a **raised CD4:CD8 ratio**.
whyNot: A neutrophilic BAL is common in IPF.
Lymphocytes and mast cells after an antigen exposure suggest HP.
Eosinophilia suggests pulmonary eosinophilia or a drug reaction.
Milky lavage fluid indicates alveolar proteinosis.

questions.stem: Five patients are being considered for antifibrotic therapy.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson’s, which patient is the most appropriate candidate?
options: Confirmed IPF with vital capacity 65% predicted
Confirmed IPF with vital capacity 92% predicted
Confirmed IPF with vital capacity 40% predicted
Cellular NSIP with vital capacity 70% predicted
Cryptogenic organising pneumonia with vital capacity 60% predicted
questions.explanation: Davidson’s offers pirfenidone or nintedanib in **IPF when VC is 50–80% predicted**.
whyNot: Above the 80% range quoted for starting treatment.
Below the 50% range quoted for starting treatment.
Cellular NSIP is steroid-responsive.
COP responds to corticosteroids.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman has taken a low-dose antibiotic every night for 2 years to prevent recurrent urinary tract infection. She now has progressive breathlessness and fine basal crackles, and HRCT shows bilateral interstitial change.
questions.leadIn: Which antibiotic is she most likely to be taking?
questions.explanation: **Nitrofurantoin** is one of the four drugs that most often cause pulmonary fibrosis, and she has taken it long term.
whyNot: Trimethoprim is not a listed cause of drug-induced pulmonary fibrosis.
Not among the listed causes of drug-induced fibrosis.
Penicillins cause idiosyncratic or eosinophilic reactions rather than chronic fibrosis.
Not among the listed causes of drug-induced fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has just been diagnosed with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. He asks about his outlook.
questions.leadIn: Which figure is most widely quoted as the median survival from diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Davidson’s quotes a **median survival of about 3 years**, with wide variation from months to many years. Other books quote 2–5 years (Kumar) or about 5 years (KC Essentials).
whyNot: Too short except in AIP or a severe exacerbation.
Too long for IPF; closer to NSIP outcomes.
Far too long; IPF is a life-limiting disease.
IPF is progressive and ultimately fatal without transplant.

questions.stem: A respiratory team is trying to decide whether a patient’s fibrotic lung disease is fibrotic NSIP or IPF.
questions.leadIn: Which feature most favours fibrotic NSIP?
options: Younger age with an associated connective tissue disease
Age over 65 years in a male ex-smoker
Extensive basal subpleural honeycombing on HRCT
questions.explanation: Fibrotic NSIP affects **younger patients, more often women**, and is often linked to **CTD**, drugs, chronic HP or HIV. Its prognosis is much better than IPF.
whyNot: Older male smokers are the typical IPF demographic.
Prominent honeycombing favours UIP/IPF; NSIP has more ground glass and minimal honeycombing.
Fibroblastic foci are a hallmark of UIP.
Relentless decline is the usual course of IPF.

ospe.identify: HRCT of **IPF**: bilateral, basal, peripheral (subpleural) reticular opacities with **honeycombing**. Confident UIP features mean biopsy is seldom needed.
CT chest in **IPF**: subpleural reticulation and **honeycomb cysts at both bases**.
**UIP pathology**: gross subpleural scarring along the posterior lower lobe (honeycomb lung), and histology of dense interstitial fibrosis with honeycomb cysts and loss of alveolar architecture.
**Non-caseating granulomas** in the lung = **sarcoidosis**, the main granulomatous DPLD (the lungs are involved in over 90% of cases).
CT of **sarcoidosis**: soft-tissue window showing **bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy**, and lung window showing multiple small nodules with reticulation.
**Finger clubbing** (enlarged, bulbous fingertip). In ILD it is common in some types, especially **IPF**, and is often a late sign.
Chest CT in **interstitial lung disease** showing **extensive pulmonary fibrosis**.
